title: Opioid overdose (adult)
subject: toxicology
summary: Support ventilation first, then give naloxone titrated to adequate breathing rather than full wakefulness (0.04 to 0.4 mg IV increments in hospital, or 0.4 to 2 mg IM, IV, SC or intranasal). Start an infusion at two-thirds of the effective reversal dose per hour if toxicity recurs, and observe until fully recovered.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Reduced consciousness, slow shallow breathing or apnoea with hypoxia, and pinpoint pupils.
Sources: heroin, morphine, fentanyl (including patches), methadone, buprenorphine, codeine-containing cough syrups, tramadol and tapentadol.
Mixed overdoses (benzodiazepines, alcohol, gabapentinoids, sedating drugs) deepen respiratory depression and may respond only partly to naloxone.
Consider other causes of coma and miosis: hypoglycaemia, head injury, pontine stroke, organophosphate or clonidine poisoning, and hypoxic brain injury.

sections.title: Airway and breathing first
items: Stimulate, open the airway, clear vomit (recovery position if breathing), and give bag-valve-mask ventilation with oxygen if breathing is inadequate; then give naloxone.
Cardiac arrest: standard CPR and advanced life support take priority; naloxone may be given but must not delay compressions, ventilation or defibrillation.
Check capillary glucose and treat hypoglycaemia (below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L)).

sections.title: Naloxone dosing
items: Goal: adequate spontaneous breathing and airway protection, not full arousal. Large doses in opioid-dependent patients cause abrupt withdrawal, vomiting and agitation.
Hospital, breathing but hypoventilating, or likely opioid-dependent: start 0.04 mg IV (up to 0.4 mg) and double the dose every 2 to 3 minutes if there is no response.

Apnoeic or peri-arrest, or no IV access: 0.4 mg IV, or 0.4 to 2 mg IM or SC, repeated every 2 to 3 minutes. In most patients 0.4 to 0.8 mg is effective (WHO); initial doses above 0.8 mg are more likely to precipitate withdrawal.
Intranasal: 1 mg (1 mL of 1 mg/mL with an atomiser) into each nostril, or a 3 to 4 mg nasal spray into one nostril; repeat every 2 to 3 minutes, alternating nostrils.
No response after a cumulative 10 mg: opioid toxicity is unlikely to be the main cause; reassess for other causes.
Buprenorphine overdose may need higher doses and early infusion because of its strong receptor binding.

Infusion if two or more boluses are needed, or after large amounts of short-acting or any long-acting or extended-release opioid: start at two-thirds of the effective (cumulative) bolus dose per hour and titrate to breathing and mental status.

sections.title: Monitoring and observation
items: Naloxone acts for about 90 to 180 minutes (half-life 30 to 45 minutes), shorter than many opioids, so re-sedation is common.
Monitor respiratory rate, SpO2 and consciousness continuously; use capnography if available.

Observe until fully recovered: at least 2 hours after the last naloxone dose after short-acting opioids such as heroin (WHO), and considerably longer after methadone, extended-release preparations, buprenorphine, fentanyl patches, or when an infusion has been needed.

sections.title: Complications and special situations
items: Precipitated withdrawal (agitation, vomiting, sweating, tachycardia): reduce by small titrated doses; protect the airway from vomit.
Rare non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema after naloxone: oxygen and ventilatory support.
Tramadol overdose can cause seizures (treat with benzodiazepines) and serotonin toxicity.
Combination products (tramadol-paracetamol, codeine-paracetamol): check a paracetamol level.
Pregnancy: give naloxone for life-threatening maternal respiratory depression, titrated to avoid acute withdrawal.

sections.title: Disposition
items: Discharge only when fully awake, breathing normally on room air, walking, and at least 2 hours after the last naloxone dose for short-acting opioids; longer for long-acting opioids.
Intentional overdose: psychiatric assessment before discharge.
Offer take-home naloxone and training for people who use opioids and their families (WHO), and referral to opioid agonist treatment and de-addiction services.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Giving naloxone before ventilating a hypoxic apnoeic patient.
Large IV boluses (for example 2 mg) to a breathing opioid-dependent patient, causing violent withdrawal and aspiration.
Discharging after a single naloxone response to a long-acting or extended-release opioid.
Assuming all coma with small pupils is opioid-related.

drugs.name: Naloxone (IV titration)
drugs.dose: 0.04 to 0.4 mg IV every 2 to 3 minutes, doubling if no response
drugs.notes: Titrate to breathing; reassess the diagnosis after 10 mg cumulative.

drugs.name: Naloxone (IM or SC)
drugs.dose: 0.4 to 2 mg, repeat every 2 to 3 minutes

drugs.name: Naloxone (intranasal)
drugs.dose: 1 mg in each nostril (1 mg/mL with atomiser) or 3 to 4 mg spray in one nostril; repeat every 2 to 3 minutes

drugs.name: Naloxone (infusion)
drugs.dose: Two-thirds of the effective cumulative bolus dose per hour IV, titrated
drugs.notes: Recurrent toxicity, long-acting or extended-release opioids, buprenorphine.

sources.title: 2023 American Heart Association Focused Update on the Management of Patients With Cardiac Arrest or Life-Threatening Toxicity Due to Poisoning
